query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation in the multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy is driven by galvanic coupling at the phase boundaries. Differential oxidation between the alternating soft fcc and hard bcc lamellae at elevated temperature produces a brittle oxide scale that is periodically removed by wear, exposing fresh material that quickly corrodes through galvanic interactions.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar structure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous mechanical sliding wear and a corrosive (oxidizing) environment at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., above 700°C) under an oxidizing, corrosive atmosphere combined with mechanical sliding contact to impose wear.
generation.structural_mediator: The heterogeneous interfaces between fcc and bcc lamellae that promote differential oxidation and facilitate galvanic coupling.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the differing oxidation kinetics of the two phases lead to the formation of non-uniform, brittle oxide scales along phase boundaries. These oxides are mechanically spalled by wear, exposing fresh surfaces that create local galvanic cells. The resulting galvanic acceleration of corrosion weakens the structure further, which in turn increases susceptibility to mechanical damage, thus creating a self-reinforcing cycle of coupled degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline homogeneous alloy, the eutectic HEA will exhibit a higher overall degradation due to an increased rate of corrosion (from galvanic effects) and higher wear rates (from the removal of brittle oxide scales). Specifically, individual measurements will show elevated mass loss, deeper wear tracks with evidence of oxide spallation, and more localized corrosion at phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: A compositionally matched single-phase high-entropy alloy exhibiting a homogeneous microstructure without distinct phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of elevated temperature, in a corrosive (oxidizing) environment concurrently with mechanical wear.
generation.uncertainty: Although the qualitative synergy between wear and corrosion is supported, the precise quantitative contributions of galvanic corrosion versus mechanical oxide spallation are uncertain and require detailed microstructural and electrochemical analysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy samples: one multi-phase eutectic HEA and one single-phase high-entropy alloy with similar overall composition. Expose both samples to identical conditions of high temperature, corrosive atmosphere, and mechanical sliding wear. Conduct post-test analyses of mass loss, wear track morphology, and oxide layer characteristics, and map local electrochemical potentials near phase boundaries.
measurements: Wear track depth and oxide spallation observations via microscopy
Corrosion penetration depth and localized chemical composition
Electrochemical mapping (e.g., using scanning Kelvin probe) to detect galvanic differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multi-phase eutectic alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in overall degradation (combined wear and corrosion) compared to the single-phase baseline, or if local galvanic effects and differential oxide formation at phase boundaries are not evident, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys

Abstract: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
